extraction.name: BoolQ
extraction.description: A reading comprehension dataset of naturally occurring yes/no questions. Each question is paired with a paragraph from Wikipedia that an independent annotator has marked as containing the answer.
extraction.creator: Christopher Clark, Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, Tom Kwiatkowski, Michael Collins, Kristina Toutanova
extraction.citeAs: Christopher Clark, Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, Tom Kwiatkowski, Michael Collins, Kristina Toutanova. BoolQ: Exploring the Surprising Difficulty of Natural Yes/No Questions. arXiv:1905.10044v1 [cs.CL] 24 May 2019
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Questions are gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine. Queries that are likely to be yes/no questions are heuristically identified. Questions are only kept if a Wikipedia page is returned as one of the first five results, in which case the question and Wikipedia page are given to a human annotator for further processing.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: User-generated content data, Software Collection, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Annotators can mark questions as 'not answerable' if the Wikipedia article does not contain the requested information.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine and Wikipedia pages.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: We combine 13k questions gathered from this pipeline with an additional 3k questions with yes/no answers from the NQ training set to reach a total of 16k questions.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Queries that are likely to be yes/no questions are heuristically identified: selecting queries where the first word is in a manually constructed set of indicator words and are of sufficient length. Questions are only kept if a Wikipedia page is returned as one of the first five results. Only questions marked as having a yes/no answer are used, and each question is paired with the selected passage instead of the entire document.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators label question/article pairs in a three-step process. First, they decide if the question is good, meaning it is comprehensible, unambiguous, and requesting factual information. Next, for good questions, annotators find a passage within the document that contains enough information to answer the question. Finally, annotators mark whether the question’s answer is 'yes' or 'no'.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Three of the authors labelled 110 randomly chosen examples. On the 110 selected examples, the answer annotations reached 90% accuracy compared to the gold-standard labels. Of the cases where the answer annotation differed from the gold-standard, six were ambiguous or debatable cases, and five were errors where the annotator misunderstood the passage.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Heuristics for identifying yes/no queries based on indicator words and length.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset has been updated since the analysis was carried out.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: Part of the value of this dataset is that it contains questions that people genuinely want to answer, tying the dataset to a clear end-task.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Yes answers are slightly more common (62.31% in the train set). There is a correlation between the nature of the question and the likelihood of a 'yes' answer. Questions were often about entertainment media.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Questions often query for complex, non-factoid information, and require difficult entailment-like inference to solve. Detecting a 'no' answer typically requires understanding that a positive assertion in the text excludes a positive assertion in the question.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, Testing, Validation, Fine Tuning for reading comprehension and natural language inference tasks.
